values: What age can my child start hockey?
What equipment do we need to begin?
Does my player need to know how to skate?
How much does it cost to get started?
What is the difference between a clinic, camp, and league?

Most KC rinks welcome skaters as young as three through introductory programs. Your child does not need to know how to skate first. Learn-to-skate classes are a friendly first step, and coaches will help you choose the right next program when they are ready.

A helmet with a full face cage, skates, shoulder and elbow pads, hockey pants, shin guards, gloves, and a stick are the usual basics. Many local programs offer equipment rentals or starter packages, so you do not need to buy everything before your first skate.

Not at all. Hockey starts with skating, stopping, and feeling comfortable on the ice. A learn-to-skate class or beginner clinic is designed for brand-new skaters and builds those skills before players join a team.

Introductory classes vary by rink, but most families can try a first session for a modest registration fee. Ask about rental equipment, seasonal packages, and scholarship options before purchasing gear. Our rink directory is a good place to compare programs.

Hockey has contact and speed, but youth programs teach body control, awareness, and safe play from day one. Properly fitted equipment, certified coaches, and age-appropriate rules are all part of a strong program. Talk with the coach about your child's experience level and comfort.

A clinic focuses on one skill or topic, like skating or shooting. A camp usually combines several skills over multiple days. A league is a season of practices and games with a team. New players often start with lessons or learn-to-skate, then move into a league when they are ready.
Start with a rink that offers learn-to-skate or beginner hockey programs.

No. Many players begin with learn-to-skate and introductory hockey before joining a league. If your child can skate, stop, and follow a coach's directions, a rink coordinator can usually point you toward the right entry-level program.
Most programs use age group and a short evaluation skate to create balanced teams. The goal is to give every player a positive challenge and a chance to contribute, not to create a perfect ranking.

A recreational season commonly includes weekly practices, scheduled games, jersey use, and optional tournaments. The exact schedule varies by rink and division, so check the registration details for your preferred facility.

Start with the rink directory to find a facility near you, then use its website or registration desk for current dates and pricing. League calendars change throughout the year, and KCHockey can help you compare options.

values: Do I need a full team to register?
What equipment do adult players need?
What level should I sign up for?

Not always. Many KC adult leagues accept individual free agents and place them on a team, while other sessions are built for established teams. Contact the rink before registration closes to ask about open spots.

Players should bring a properly fitted helmet with a full cage or shield, skates, gloves, shoulder and elbow pads, hockey pants, shin guards, socks, and a stick. Your league may have additional safety requirements.

Be honest about your skating, pace, and playing experience. Recreational leagues are welcoming to newer adults, while intermediate and advanced divisions are better for players with established game experience. A league director can help place you.

Adult league games run at rinks across the metro, including facilities in Overland Park, Independence, Liberty, Olathe, and Blue Springs. Use the rink directory to see what is closest to home or work.
Low-pressure games, new friends, and a reason to leave work on time. A great place to get back on the ice or learn the adult game.
Competitive enough to matter and friendly enough to grab a drink afterward. Balanced teams keep every shift moving.
Fast, structured hockey for players who want a serious skate and a full 60 minutes of pace.
